> There are two ways to approach this.

> 1. Instead of standardizing your covariates ahead of time, have unmarked do the work for you by putting scale() in the formulas, e.g.
>
> occu(~scale(area)~scale(road), umf).
>
> Then when using predict, supply the newdata on the original (non-standardized) covariate scale, and combine the newdata and the results from predict when making the plot.
>
> 2. If you standardize the covariates yourself first, as you have done, it's a little harder. After fitting the model, create a covariate range to plot (x), on the original scale. Then standardize this range *using the same values for the mean and SD used to standardize the original dataset*. Supply the standardized range of values x_scaled to the predict newdata argument. Then plot the results of predict (y) vs. the original covariate range (x). If you have other non-focal covariates in the model you are holding constant, you need to standardize them the same way before putting them in the newdata, using the mean and SD values from the original dataset.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A long-term mammal monitoring programme will begin in Spain in the coming year. The goal is to generate national-scale distribution probability maps for each species using hierarchical models and data from detection-non-detection sampling. It is a long-distance race, and we are still brainstorming about the survey protocols (repeated surveys, multiple observers, etc.) and modelling framework (static/dynamic occupancy models, integrated models if different data sources are necessary/advisable, etc.).

We know that occupancy models were used in Switzerland for the Swiss Breeding Bird Atlas. Are you aware of other large-scale (state/national) monitoring projects using hierarchical models to account for imperfect detectability? Any assistance or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!
Best,

Simone

messages.subject: Variable selection in dynamic occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: Variable selection in dynamic occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am sorry, if this question was posted before, but I couldn't seem to find it.

I am relatively new to occupancy modelling and currently trying to fit dynamic occupancy models to camera trap data using unmarked. I have data from 64 camera trap locations that were sampled over 6 years (primary periods) and the presence/absence data was grouped into 16 secondary survey periods (weeks) for at least 6 different species, that I want to model independently from each other, to understand what drove occupancy dynamics.

Now, I am running into some problems trying to fit a model or rather finding the right variables to include in a model. My data includes both Observation Covariates such as climate data and Site Covariates, such as habitat/vegetation data, elevation, distance to urban settlements, etc., that for some sites change between years, therefore I included them as yearlySiteCovs. Before analysis, I checked my variables for multicollinearity and correlation and removed the respective variables from my analysis. I still end up with quite a few potential variables (11 SiteCovs and 4 ObsCovs) for the potential models.

As I couldn't find a function to do the model selection automatically, I tried to use a backwards elimination approach starting with a global model including all potential variables and removing the most insignificant independent variables, for each detection, occupancy, colonization and extinction, until there is only significant variables left in the model and then fitted a "final" model. Yet, when I analyse the goodness of fit using the mb.gof.test function, it seems that those models are terribly overdispersed, e.g. my Chi² as well as my c-hat values are even Infinite for some species/models. I also tried a more automated modelling approach, where I fit every possible model with every possible combinations of variables and chose the one with the lowest AIC, but the resulting models are even worse.

There weren't any convergence problems with my models and I only have those major problems for 3 out of 6 species (for the remaining 3 species the backwards elimination approach at least led to models with an okayish GOF, i.e. c-hat < 3). The number of observations for the respective species doesn't seem to be the driving factor here, as those problems occur for species with many observations as well as for species with few observations.

I am not sure, if my variable selection approach is even the right one or if there is a better way to this, rather than doing a backwards elimination or AIC selection. I would be glad, to receive any suggestions on how I could do this in a way that hopefully helps me find some better models.

Thank you very much!
Best,
Annika

messages.body_plain:
Dear Hendrik,

I really think that before we even ask a statistical question about which technique is better, we ought to ALWAYS state our biological questions. That is, the objectives of our statistical analysis. Without objectives, we can’t define what procedure is best. But since I always forget all this myself, I am not going to make a big deal of it now 😊

OK, so there is no problem at all using the dynamic model. It is actually better in two respects than using 4 static models (or one static model with a 4-level factor “Year”):
It gives you insight into the two processes that underlie changes in a species distribution: colonization and extinction
And by doing this, the model also corrects for temporal autocorrelation in the data

On the other hand, it is a more complex model, and all else equal, we ought to always use the simpler model. So, if you’re really not interested in the dynamics rates (col and ext), I might perhaps use occu() and not worry about temporal autocorrelation.

About the covariates: if you think they are mostly stable across the 4 years you might perhaps still add them as site covariates. If you find effects of them, then you can be almost sure than in reality these effects would be even more pronounced, since errors in x-variables lead to an attenuation of the slope estimates towards zero of covariates in a regression model.

Finally, different methods should not be a problem if the two kinds really sample the same statistical population of sites in a random way. Then, Method would just be a detection covariate with two levels. That’s one of the great things about these hierarchical models: you can neatly separate the process and the observation of the process.

Best regards  -- Marc

Dear Marc,

thank you very much for your answer.

The biological question is as follows. It is about gaining a better understanding of the presence and absence of the species. It was considered extinct in this area for a long time and was only rediscovered a few years ago and a monitoring programme has been running since then. An occupancy model can shed light on these issues and provide a more robust and accurate estimate of species abundance and distribution. This is part of my Master's thesis.

It is unfortunately not possible to distinguish between the nest box data and trapping data; I have previously considered this a weakness of the data base - what you say sounds very plausible though. The only covariate I would project with any degree of certainty to a period four and a half years ago would be tree density - this is likely to be fairly invariant. Likewise, the number of tree species in the transect should have remained stable. That would make two. Last year, however, not all sampling points were sampled at the same frequency - again, this is another variable that makes it considerably more difficult for me to create an adequate data basis at the moment.

My idea was: year 1 - 3 to create an occupancy model without covariates and for the fourth year to create a regression (e.g. binary logistic regression, as it currently lends itself due to the data sorting). However, your arguments have convinced me to look at the "constant" variables again.

The data come from >70 sampling sites. In fact, most of the time the traps are also set at a nest box site. Over the years, nest boxes remained unmoved and traps were (mostly) placed at the same sampling points (300 trapping nights per session).

I am currently leaning towards the occu() function and thus the "simpler" model.

I am delighted that I was able to get help so quickly.

Best regards

Hendrik

It is unfortunately not possible to distinguish between the nest box data and trapping data; I have previously considered this a weakness of the data base - what you say sounds very plausible though. The only covariate I would project with any degree of certainty to a period four and a half years ago would be tree density - this is likely to be fairly invariant. I am currently leaning towards the occu() function and thus the "simpler" model.

Dear Hendrik,

you don’t have to include method as a covariate. Moreover, you said that at many sites, for many occasions, both methods are employed simultaneously.

And yes, you may absolutely work with occu() with your kinds of covariates.

One additional thought though: when stacking the data year-wise and then using occu(), you might want to fit a random site effect to accommodate possible non-independence of occupancy at the same site over multiple years. For many of the model-fitting functions in unmarked, this can now be done, since Ken Kellner added the TMB software as an engine with which to fit models in unmarked. You can now use lme4- (or glmmTMB-)like notation to specify models with random effects. For instance, to fit an occupancy model with random site effects in occupancy (and constant detection), you would do this:

fm <- occu(~1 ~ (1|site), umf)

(I note that you must have data from multiple years to be able to fit a random site effect in occupancy. With data from just a single year, the associated variance parameter IS NOT ESTIMABLE.)

This random-effects option is really great. For instance, it would also allow to fit random observer effects in detection in the analysis of citizen-science data sets collected by many observers (provided observer ID is known).

Best regards  -- Marc

> > > And by doing this, the model also corrects for temporal autocorrelation in the data
> > >

> > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This group has been exceptionally helpful so far from all the past conversations, but alas I have finally encountered something that I cannot find an answer to in previous conversations.

I am working with a relatively small dataset using single season occupancy (n=204 with 66 observations) that had been giving me issues in terms of parameter estimates and SE's. The more complex models were producing a great amount of boundary estimates and this was an issue since I am more concerned with inference gained from parameters in my study than predictions back to the site levels. I recently looked into the occuPEN_CV method of model fitting and it appears that most of my issues have been resolved (better estimates, more what I expected considering the biology of my intended species). I have read the Hutchinson et al. 2015 paper and from their results, I plan to use the 'Ridge' penalty type since this method most often found estimates closest to the true values.

My question is how to go about model selection with this procedure. From what I have read it appears that AICc should no longer be used since this is already a form of penalized likelihood. I have seen recommendations of using the highest cross-validated score to compare models, with the highest score being the most supported. This makes sense since more complex models are likely to impose a greater penalty, making straight AIC comparison biased. I have seen the recent code posted to assess the CV scores in occuMulti(), but I am wondering how I could apply this approach with an unmarkedFitOccuPEN_CV object. Any assistance would be greatly appreciated.

Another question is how to obtain SE's and CI's for the predict() function using this method of model fitting. I have followed recommendations to use nonparboot to obtain SE's of the paramters in the model, but I am unsure of how to either bind these to the fitted model object to use predict normally or add these as an additional argument in the call to predict(). Again, any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks!

Aaron

messages.body_plain:
Dear Hanna,

couple of comments:
Normally I’d analyse both data sets together and simply treat the detection method as a covariate for detection. Although: this assumes that both methods sample space in the same way, e.g., it would not be good if you have one method in the forest and the other in the open.
When using colext, you can estimate one occupancy parameter for the start, i.e. for year 1, and then one set of colonization and extinction params. You have only a single annual interval, and these params governing the dynamics are defined per interval, not per year. In other words, you then have only spatial variation in col and ext, but not temporal variation
Thus, since there is only a single col and ext parameter, you cannot have yearly site covariates on them, but only site covariates
If you want to use site covariates to explain spatial variation in col and ext, it would probably make most sense to use covariates that are measured during the first year or else during the annual interval, but not during the second year
For the cameras, I’d probably aggregate daily data to weekly data. This makes the data set more manageable and will reduce the temporal autocorrelation that might otherwise exist (and which cannot be taken into account in colext).
You can’t compare the AIC between occu() and colext() since the likelihood differs
Overall, I have to say, that if you’re not particularly interested in explaining the change (and you can do it with one of the data sets only anyway), I’d probably use occu() on a stacked data analysis.

Best regards  --- Marc

So I've been reading more about assessing model fit in the respective Chapter of MacKenzie et al. (2017) and I think I have an idea of what causes my problems with calculating Chi² and c-hat. Please, correct me if I got any of this wrong:
As I have 16 secondary survey periods, I have 2^16 (65,635) possible detection histories. Since my number of surveyed units (64) is relatively small compared to the number of possible detection histories, the expected number of cameras with a particular detection history is also extremely small, which results in my huge Chi² values. Additionally, I have a lot of NAs in my dataset due to camera failure/malfunction/theft/etc. Which I guess, increases the number of potential detection histories even more, causing even larger Chi² values and accordingly also huge c-hat values.

1. Why do I get much better model fit statistics for some species? The number of survey periods, survey units and missing values is exactly the same for all species, so I don't understand why for some of them the model fit is more or less okay, while for others it is completely terrible. If my theory with the large number of potential detection histories is correct, shouldn't it cause poor model fit for all species?

2. What can I potentially do to account for this problems? I already grouped the observations into weekly presence/absence data to reduce the number of secondary survey periods. Would it make sense to group it into even larger time intervals (e.g. months) or analyse only a subset of my data, e.g. 6 weeks instead of 16 weeks?

Dear Hanna,

you have (at least) two ways of viewing your data: either via a static model which has one parameter of occupancy in year 1 and another in year 2. You can fit such a model using occu() by treating Year as a factor. Or, as a dynamic model where you have one occupancy parameter in year 1 and then an extinction (eps) and colonization (gamma) parameter for the transition from year 1 to year 2. This model you can fit with colext(). In a sense, the pair of (eps, gamma) in the dynamic model replaces the occupancy parameter in the second year from the first model (the one you fit with with occu()).

So, I suggest to think very clearly about the chronology of events in the occupancy process, along with the possible covariates. In the model you can fit with occu(), you have two parameters at time points 1 and 2. In the model that you fit with colext(), you have one parameter at time 1 and two more that belong somewhere to time 1.5. So, (unless near- or totally constant over time) a covariate that you measure in year 2 is unlikely to be a sensible predictor for spatial variation in the dynamics parameters (eps, gamma), since at the time when you measure this covariate, the state transition has already taken place.

Perhaps it helps if you make some pictures of the temporal dynamics of the processes in question ?

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we're fitting some dynamic occupancy models to a 126 site x 26 year data set. Ext and col is both very low, and p is very high, so from a model with year-specific fixed effects in unmarked we get LOTS of estimates that are on the boundary (i.e., 0 or 1).

So we went to ubms instead and tried stan_colext(), which conveniently has about 99% the same syntax as colext() in unmarked, but uses the Bayesian engine Stan under the hood. We fitted the same fixed-effects model as in unmarked. This takes about 21 min on my laptop (compared to about half of that time in unmarked) and produces no boundary estimates. By taking the posterior mean rather than the mode in a Bayesian analysis one is almost guaranteed not to get them.

Attached is a plot that shows estimates vs. truth for a single simulated data set for unmarked and for ubms and then a comparison of Bayes vs. MLE. In that last plot, MLEs on the boundary can be well seen at the bottom left and the top right.

So, all of this looks quite nice, but I have two questions:
We got this error message from ubms; any ideas what it means ?
Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)) :
  error in evaluating the argument 'i' in selecting a method for function '[': argument "submodel" is missing, with no default
I'd like to get an estimate of the total population size for each year, which in our case is the sum of occupied sites in every year. In unmarked I can get this by issuing this obscure command:
nocc.hat <- colSums(ranef(fm)@post[,2,])

Any chance to get this from ubms as well ?

Thanks a lot and best regards  --- Marc

Ken
